speakeroldname: Hon. R. J. MANION (Minister of Railways) :
speechtext:
I think I will have to make a few remarks in reply to that question. The Prince Edward Island car ferry has been operated in the past iby the Canadian National Railways as part of eastern lines, and whatever deficit there has been on it has been absorbed into the eastern lines' deficit. There has been a great deal of pressure, as my hon. friend probably knows, from Prince Edward Island chambers of commerce and various other bodies who seem to desire very strongly that so far as accounting is concerned it should be dealt with by the government itself, while operation is still handled by the Canadian National Railways. At their request, and after a great deal of pressure,-because frankly I did not see any advantage in it myself-it has been arranged that in the future, while the Canadian National Railways will still handle the ferry as they have in the past, the accounting will be separate and the estimate for the deficit on the operation of the ferry, if any, will be submitted to the house as a separate estimate.

Hon. C. H. CAHAN (Secretary of State) moved the second reading of Bill No. 107, respecting a certain trade agreement between Canada and France.
He said:	Mr. Speaker, this bill is framed
to approve of the trade arrangement between Canada and France which was signed at Ottawa on the 12th of May of this year. It is within the knowledge of the house that the former trade agreement, which was signed in 1922, was terminated in June of last year, and this is a new agreement to provide for reciprocal tariffs on the exchange of goods between the two countries in substitution for the agreement which was terminated.

Canada-France Trade Agreement
The house is well aware that since 1892, when Mr. Maline made his celebrated report to the French government, France has been one of the most highly protected countries in Europe or, I think, in the world. When that report was made the basis of the French tariff law France became predominantly protective in its tariff policy, and in that year established its new schedules under which there was a maximum general tariff and also a minimum tariff applicable to all imports into France. Especially in respect to agricultural products has France been highly protected. It has been the policy of France ever since 1892 to protect its own agricultural products with a view to making that country independent of the rest of the world, especially with regard to wheat and other grains, in case a national emergency should arise, and the French people again be called to arms. It is a very significant fact that, going back for scores of years and in fact for centuries, no man has reached the age of fifty-five or sixty in France who has not seen that country over-run by foreign troops in an attempt to subjugate that nation. France has felt unable to protect its supplies of food coming from overseas, and therefore has insisted on maintaining a highly protective policy for the purpose of encouraging the production of food supplies within its own boundaries. Those hon. gentlemen who have gone through France, as I have on many occasions, will remember passing through miles and miles of wheat fields which compare not only well but very favourably indeed with the best wheat fields of our western country.
Prior to 1892, when France adopted these maximum and minimum tariffs, Canada had no trade arrangement with that country. Our trade and commercial arrangements were governed up to that time by treaties or conventions which had been negotiated by the government of the United Kingdom and which applied to us as they did to the other dominions, colonies and possessions of Great Britain. But after this new tariff was adopted Sir Charles Tupper, then High Commissioner for Canada at London, proceeded to Paris and on behalf of the government of Canada concluded negotiations for the first trade treaty with France, which was signed by the British ambassador and by Sir Charles Tupper, on behalf of Canada, on February 6, 1893. This trade treaty was subsequently approved by the Canadian parliament in 1894.
Under the provision of that trade arrangement Canada secured the French minimum tariff on some nineteen staple Canadian products in return for concessions made by Canada, by way of reduction of our Canadian import duties on wines, soaps and a number of other products of France. But after 1893 Canadian industrial and agricultural production increased very rapidly and became more diversified than before, and the agreement which was ratified by Canada in 1895 came to be regarded with more or less dissatisfaction in this country. Further negotiations then ensued between the two countries after the close of a colonial conference at London in 1902, at which it was practically decided that this dominion would grant special preferences to Great Britain which would not be granted to foreign countries. But after the return of Sir Wilfrid Laurier from the colonial conference of 1902 the French government insisted that no modification of the existing trade arrangement with France would be made unless Canada would concede to France the same low preferential rates, which had been conceded to Great Britain, and which were comprised in the so-called "British preferential tariff." The government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier however refused to make this concession, and so for a time the negotiations continued and finally failed. But in 1907 the government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier resumed negotiations with France, and on September 19 of that year a new convention was signed at Paris by the British ambassador and by Mr. Fielding, then Minister of Finance, and Mr. Brodeur, a minister of the crown, I have forgotten his office-
Minister of Marine.

Yes, Minister of Marine and Fisheries, on behalf of Canada. Owing to the opposition of the French Senate, which still continued, this convention was further modified and amended by a supplemental convention, signed January 23, 1909, and this amended convention of 1907-09 was then approved and came into force on February 1, 1910. The list of Canadian products entering France under the French minimum tariff was extended by this trade convention, and France, Algeria and the French colonies received the benefit of Canada's intermediate tariff which had then been established.
These arrangements continued until after the close of the great war, when, the French tariff having been increased from time to time, it was found that the high general tariff of France had practically precluded numerous industrial and agricultural products of Canada from access to the French market. The Canadian government then proposed to grant to all French products the advantages of Canada's intermediate tariff in return for the grant of the French minimum tariff to a more extended list of Canadian products. This the

Canada-France Trade Agreement
French government of the day refused to concede, and on the recommendation of the Minister of Trade and Commerce the convention of 1907-09 was denounced by Canada on March 19, 1920, and terminated on June 19, 1920. The following year, further negotiations between the governments of the two countries resulted in a modus vivendi or temporary arrangement being concluded at Paris on January 29, 1921. Broadly speaking, this temporary arrangement was based on the convention then recently terminated. Twenty-six new items were included in this arrangement on terms more favourable to Canada, but a number of Canadian products then received less favourable rates from France, being removed from the French minimum rate and granted new tariff rates which were intermediate between the French minimum tariff and the French maximum tariff.
In the following summer of 1922 the Hon. W. S. Fielding, then Minister of Finance, and the then Minister of Marine and Fisheries, the present distinguished member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) negotiated a new convention with France which was signed at Paris on December 15, 1922, by the British ambassador and by the two Canadian ministers mentioned. This new trade convention was approved by parliament and brought into force on September 5, 1923. Under its terms Canada afforded to France fixed tariff rates on a number of items substantially lower than Canada's intermediate tariff, so that thereafter there were fixed rates on thirty-one items or parts of items on the Canadian tariff, lower than the intermediate tariff rates then prevailing; and this new 'arrangement also conceded to France Canada's intermediate tariff rates, less a discount of ten per cent on ninety-one items or parts of items, and intermediate rates decreased by a discount of fifteen per cent on three items. In addition, Canada granted to France complete most favoured nation treatment in respect of all tariff matters. In return France granted its minimum tariff on one hundred and forty-one tariff items, a considerable number of which-I say this without special criticism-covered chemical and other products which have never since been produced in Canada, and on other items certain percentages of reduction in the maximum general tariff of France.
Canada was also then accorded better tariff treatment in the French colonies, and provision was made for Canadian products receiving, on importation into France, any tariff concessions then made or thereafter to be made by France to the United States of America. Under this convention of 1922

France retained the unfettered right to increase all or any of her tariff rates, minimum or maximum, at will, without consulting Canada.- Widespread increases in French maximum and minimum rates have been the outstanding characteristic of the French tariff policy since that convention came into force.
In April and August of 1926, there was a general increase in French customs rates aggregating approximately sixty-nine per cent of the rates in force on nearly all commodities. These rates were effected for the purpose of readjusting French customs tariff protection to French national industry and production. Later, the French tariff revision of September 6, 1927, not only reclassified numerous sections of the French tariff but also established maximum and minimum rates considerably higher than those which had previously been in force. For example-I trust the house will allow this digression because it is of real significance under present conditions-since 1926 the French minimum customs duty on Canadian wheat and other wheat products has been raised on four different occasions. Expressing these increases in the equivalent of Canadian currency it will be ascertained that on September 3, 1927, the previously existing rate was increased to 17^ cents per bushel; by November 18, 1927, the rate had been increased to 27 cents per bushel; by May 24, 1929, it had been increased to 37 cents per bushel; by May 20, 1930, to 33 cents per bushel and since May 20, 1930, to 85 cents per bushel. These were all increases in the minimum tariff of France. The maximum rate or the general tariff was made twice the minimum rate and on the importations of wheat into France from Canada it stands to-day at approximately $1.70 per bushel. The increases I have mentioned, that is those up to 85 cents per bushel, were made in the minimum tariff to which Canada was entitled under the convention then in force. Since June of last year when that treaty was terminated, as I said before, Canadian wheat has been subjected to the maximum tariff rate which is the equivalent of $1.70 per bushel in Canadian currency.
Under the French law of December 1, 1929, importations of foreign wheat into France have been restricted by prescribing the percentages of domestic and foreign wheat which may lawfully be used in making flour to be used for bread making. The percentages of foreign wheat which have been prescribed from time to time for domestic use have varied according to the supplies of domestic wheat available. When I was in France, only three per cent of foreign wheat was permitted

Canada-France Trade Agreement
to be used, but, at the present time, by a decree recently passed, I understand that this percentage of foreign wheat has been reduced from three to one per cent. While I was in France carrying on these negotiations the fall in wheat prices on the French domestic market which then averaged, as the exchange fluctuated, from $1.25 to $1.30 per bushel in Canadian money, had caused such widespread resentment in the agricultural communities throughout France that at one time it was thought the life of the government would be seriously endangered. One afternoon I attended at the Chamber of Deputies when this matter was being discussed and I noticed that a large number of deputies representing agricultural communities were strong in their denunciation of the government for allowing the price of wheat to fall as low as the equivalent in our money of $1.25 per bushel.
In 1931, under the auspices of the League of Nations, France entered into an agreement known as the Stresa convention. This convention has been published in the reports of the League of Nations and I fancy tha.t nearly every member of the house who is interested in agricultural production and especially wheat production is familiar with its terms. Under the terms of this convention France agreed to exceptional and temporary measures in order to assist Hungary and Jugoslavia. Later on, the terms of this convention were extended to Roumania. A rebate of thirty per cent of the minimum tariff on wheat imported into France was allowed to these three countries. This convention granted to each of these three countries the privilege of supplying ten per cent of the annual importations of wheat into France. Therefore, at the present time thirty per cent of the total annual importations of wheat into France is obtained from these three countries of central Europe.
During the discussions which ensued, especially with regard to wheat items, I learned that France was vigorously encouraging the production of wheat in her colonies in northern Africa. The importations of wheat from Algeria, Tunis and Morocco increased from 14,000,000 bushels in 1931 to 24,000,000 bushels last year. Although I have no personal knowledge of the facts, it was stated to me in these conversations that the department of agriculture of France was encouraging the sowing of hard wheat in Algeria. The result has been that France is receiving an independent supply of hard wheat of practically the same standard as that previously imported from Canada. In talking this over with a gentleman who had expert knowledge
of wheat growing I was told' that unless France imported new seed from Canada from time to time she would be unable to keep up the production of hard wheat in Algeria. Because of the climate and the soil of that country, if the wheat produced is sown again from year to year it becomes more in the nature of soft than hard wheat. There is a gradual deterioration in the hardness of the wheat. These are matters with regard to which I am not capable of giving the house an expert opinion, save this. That, as wheat forms by far the largest part in value of Canada's annual exports to France, I have stressed the difficulties which we have, to meet in that market for this important product and I also state that the question of retaining the minimum tariff for Canadian wheat in the French market was one of the greatest difficulties that beset me during the negotiations.
But to return to the trade convention of 1922, France thereafter negotiated with Germany a new trade convention which came into force on December 15, 1928, and by which Germany received from France complete most-favoured nation treatment, and owing to the competition which then ensued Canadian products were by the Franco-German treaty subjected to more severe competition in many lines in the French market. Coincident with the negotiation of this Franco-German treaty, the French government further increased their minimum and maximum rates on many Canadian products which had been included in our Canadian convention of 1922 and thus increased the customs payable on those Canadian products entering the French market. Moreover, as I have already stated, while France under the 1922 convention with Canada was at complete liberty to raise her tariff rates at will, Canada had granted to France fixed tariff rates on thirty-one items or parts of items of our tariff which were substantially lower than our intermediate rates, and by reason [DOT] of these fixed rates and of the fact that by successive trade agreements Canada had granted most-favoured foreign nation treatment to twenty-three other countries, the whole tariff structure of this country was, in respect of those favoured fixed items, anchored and immovable, so that as long as the convention of 1922 remained in force, Canada was unable to increase her tariff on those items in respect of her imports from twenty-two or twenty-three other countries.
It was therefore deemed essential by this government that Canada should recover freedom of action in tariff matters. Early in February, 1931, the Canadian government sought to obtain satisfactory modifications of

Canada-France Trade Agreement
the terms of the French trade agreement of 1922 and, failing in this endeavour, this government on December 15, 1931, gave to France six months' notice of the termination of the convention of 1922. At the same time Canada offered to France to enter immediately upon the negotiation of a new trade convention which might be deemed more satisfactory to both countries. The old trade convention therefore terminated on June 16, 1932. Although in the meantime the Canadian government had proposed an interim arrangement to December 31, 1932, on the basis of granting to France, during this interim, most-favoured national treatment for her products in Canada, the French government refused to consent to such an interim arrangement.
It was under these circumstances that, as I was leaving Canada to attend the general assembly of the League of Nations in September last, I was authorized by the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett), who is also Secretary of State for External Affairs, to open, on behalf of the government, conversations with the government of France regarding a new commercial convention between the two countries. In September, therefore, on my way to Geneva, with the assistance and cooperation of the Hon. Philippe Roy, Canadian Minister at Paris, who certainly has a very intimate knowledge of French political affairs and a close acquaintance and friendship with nearly every prominent statesman in France, I met the French Premier, the Minister of Commerce and some of the important officials of the French Department of Foreign Affairs. It was agreed that these conversations would be renewed after my return to Paris at the close of the general assembly of the League of Nations.
The negotiations with the French government commenced effectively in October of last year and were continued with the government of Mr. Herriot until it was defeated in the French chamber in November last. The negotiations thereafter continued with the government of Mr. Paul Boncourt who succeeded Mr. Herriot as premier, and they were practically concluded, except with regard to three or four contentious items under discussion which remained to be settled, as we anticipated, on the morning of January 28 last. We terminated the session of the commission on the 26th to resume on the 27th. On the 27th a crisis arose and I was unable to see the Premier and the Minister of Commerce who had promised to receive me that afternoon. The Minister of Commerce promised to see me later, during the recess

between seven and eight o'clock, and then I received word that owing to a crisis having arisen, a caucus of his party had been called for the recess and that our meeting had to be postponed. I was awakened early the following morning from my sleep by the private secretary of one of the ministers to tell me that the discussion had continued all night; that the government had been voted out of office at six o'clock that morning and that they had handed in their resignation at seven o'clock. We therefore initialled the various items agreed to and left, I think, three or four items for further discussion.
I then returned to Canada and after my return a new government was formed with Mr. Deladier as premier. Since that date the negotiations have been concluded, resulting in this trade arrangement and in the other convention. This has been greatly due to the kindly offices of that very estimable gentleman who occupies the position of French Minister at Ottawa and who certainly has devoted himself unsparingly to bringing about a satisfactory trade arrangement between the two countries. I have to pay him a high tribute for his kindness and courtesy to me during the remainder of the negotiations.
Under this new trade arrangement, products coming from France enumerated in schedule C, including seventy-seven tariff items, will enjoy the intermediate tariff of Canada with a discount of 10 per cent therefrom. On fifteen tariff items a higher discount than 10 per cent is granted. Under this arrangement there are no increases on importations into Canada. In respect of seven items, the British preferential tariff is granted, especially in respect to books printed in France in the French language, surgical instruments and scientific apparatus, cinematograph and moving picture films made in France and speaking the French language, while certain articles of special religious significance are admitted to this country free. In respect of certain imports admitted under the same rate as the British preferential tariff, it will be noted that these items will come into force when authorized by order in council. Several of these items, especially books and surgical instruments, seemingly conflict with the Ottawa conference trade agreement between Great Britain and Canada. But during the negotiation of this trade arrangement assurances were received from the government of the United Kingdom that there would be no objection to the inclusion of these ispecial articles in the trade agreement with France. I therefore inserted a proviso in regard to these items coming into force by order in council, in order that official recognition of

Canada-France Trade Agreement
these concessions might be first obtained from the government of the United Kingdom. I think there is a clear understanding with regard to these matters.
Schedule D contains a supplementary list of tariff items in respect to which French products will enjoy Canada's intermediate tariff. This trade arrangement will be approved and confirmed, if this bill becomes law. As hon. members will notice, it is a provisional agreement which is made pending the conclusion of a commercial convention which will regulate in a more complete and permanent manner tradie relations between Canada and France. There were insurmountable difficulties in the way of concluding a more permanent convention, these difficulties being due chiefly to the application of the French minimum tariff to Canadian wheat, and due also to the fact that international monetary policy has not been so stabilized as to enable the respective governments to determine on what basis duties will be levied when imported into either one country or the other. I do not wish to repeat statements about the proposed London economic conference, but it was felt by the Canadian representative that, owing to the wheat conference which was then likely to take place, and is now being held at Geneva, and owing to the subject matter of wheat being one which will come under discussion at London, it was better to arrive at a provisional agreement capable of giving temporary satisfaction than to attempt at this stage to procure a permanent trade convention with France. This trade arrangement is made for the fixed period of one year from May 12, 1933, the date on which it was signed. It may be terminated on May 12, 1934, by either party giving prior notice to the other to that effect on or before February 12, 1934. This trade arrangement may be extended beyond May 12, 1934, by the tacit consent of both parties. If it is continued after May 12, 1934, by tacit consent it may be terminted by either party giving the other three months' notice to that effect.
To this statement one exception is made in respect of No. 68 of the French tariff, which deals with wheat. That exception is to the effect that wheat and other wheat products included in tariff item No. 68 shall enjoy the French minimum tariff for the duration of the present agreement, which is fixed for one year from the date of its signature, with a proviso that not later than March 31, 1934, the two governments will examine together the conditions under which France may find it possible to extend beyond May 12, 1934, this concession of its minimum tariff to Canadian
wheat. Moreover another exception is contained in the note attached to schedule A to the effect that a quota of 25,000 quintals of canned salmon will be effective until October 1, of the present year. France has entered into an arrangement with Japan with respect to a supply of canned salmon, and until October 1 next it was impossible, except by violating that convention, to grant to Canada a quota larger than 25,000 quintals.
Is that the League of Nations quintal or the British quintal?
French quintals.
One hundred pounds?

I shall have to look that
up. As a matter of fact I did not know there was a League of Nations quintal. The one in question however is the European and continental measurement. They agreed that on October 1 of this year they will arrange a new quota. That quota will be arranged on the basis of the French quota law, and will be determined by exportations made from Canada to France in the years 1927, 1928, 1929 and 1930. I find that under this tariff arrangement the quintal is equal to 220 pounds. Moreover, with regard to canned lobsters I find we are entitled to an annual quota of 3,000 quintals. Under this trade arrangement Canadian products mentioned in schedule A covering 185 items will enjoy the French minimum tariff. Canadian products mentioned in schedule B covering sixty-five other items will enjoy percentages of reduction in the French general tariff which are specified in schedule B. Provision is also made with respect to exportation of Canadian products to the French colonies and territories. The French colonies are divided into two main groups. The first group comprises the assimilated colonies to which the French customs tariff applies. This group includes Algeria, Indo-C'hina, Madagascar and its dependencies, Mayotte and Camores, Guadaloupe and its dependencies, Martinique, French Guiana and Reunion.
The second group, whose tariffs are not assimilated to that of France, that is, which have a special tariff of their own, includes St. Pierre and Miquelon, Tunis, Morocco, Syria and Lebanon, French West Africa, including Senegal, French Guiana, Mauritania, Ivory Coast, Dahomey, French Sudan, High Volta and Niger. Other colonies not assimilated are French Equatorial Africa, Gabun, Togoland, Oameroons, French Somaliland, French settlements in India, French Oceania, New Hebrides and New Caledonia.

Canada-France Trade Agreement
Under these trade arrangements the Canadian products mentioned in schedule A which enjoy the French minimum tariff in France when imported into the French colonies which are termed assimilated, that is colonies which have the same customs tariff as France, will enjoy the minimum tariff, whether this is the French customs minimum tariff or the minimum special colonial tariff then in force in that colony. Canadian products mentioned in schedule B on importation into the French colonies whose tariff is assimilated to that of France will enjoy the percentages of reduction on the general or maximum tariff mentioned in schedule B whether that tariff is the French tariff or a special colonial tariff. In the French colonies which are not assimilated, that is, which do not come under t'he French tariff, as well as in all French protectorates, the products of Canada enumerated in both schedules A and B will enjoy the lowest customs tariff a/pplicable to such goods, no matter what may be their origin.
I suppose that in looking ahead one cannot altogether ignore the advantage of Canadian products having access to the territories of France. Spread as they are throughout the world, they represent a population of sixty millions of people. According to the last statistics available to me their annual imports were $707,000,000 or S70S.000.000 of our money, and their exports $588,000,000 of our money, representing a total trade of nearly $1,300,000,000. We have participated in this trade to a certain extent, but I think not exceeding $1,000,000 to $1,500,000-1 thought I had the statistics at hand, but I have not at the moment. The opinion prevalent in the discussions which I had with the commission, which was composed of official representatives of the French Foreign Office, the Finance department, the Commercial department and the departments of Agriculture and Colonies, was that in many of these colonies Canada had rare opportunities for advancing its trade.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I do not think it necessary to proceed further to discuss the items of these schedules. I .would only remind the house that under the conditions which now prevail throughout the world it must be conceded that I met with exceptional difficulties in the prolonged discussions which took place at Paris. In those discussions I trust I was not unduly anxious to secure a new trade arrangement with France by reason of the fact that I am one of the ministers of the crown in this government representing the province of Quebec, which province by racial ties and speech and intimate social intercourse has special affinities for France and a desire

to maintain the most cordial relations between Canada and France, though I was not unmindful of such considerations. Moreover I can say with all frankness that whether I succeeded to your satisfaction or not I gave to these negotiations all my heart and mind and strength. I did the best I could, and perhaps I am egotistical enough to think that I did as well as could possibly have been done under the conditions which confronted me.

Those of us sitting to your left, Mr. Speaker, can naturally have no objection to a treaty being made with the republic of France. We accept the principle of a treaty with any country if by that treaty better trade can be developed between two parts of the world.
The provisions of the agreement are long and intricate. As to the actual terms of the agreement made by the Secretary of State and the actual terms of the agreement which it supersedes, there is practically no difference, as I propose to show in a few moments.
I do not object that the minister has given us such a careful and lengthy review of the treaty, but I do object to a treaty of such magnitude being presented at such a late hour in the session as to make it utterly impossible to give to it the careful study that it deserves. It is only because it is a provisional agreement that we probably should not expect to go into it as thoroughly as if it were a fixed agreement for a term of years. The minister points out that the old treaty could be terminated on six months' notice. That is quite true, it was an indeterminate treaty, but on three months' notice either party could terminate it. I cannot see a particle of difference between these terms of the old and the terms of the new treaty. The minister states that this treaty is for a year, but by tacit consent, whatever that means it will continue in force. I figure that this means that if nothing is said the treaty goes on. It can however be ter-

minated by notice, in three months' time. As to any criticism that might be made in committee on the rates of duty applicable to any of the items, I doubt if criticism can be very well founded. I am sure the minister agrees with me that it will take at least a year to find out what the workings of the customs tariff will be on many of these items. At the present time importers find it absolutely impossible to get information as to what merchandise will cost when it arrives in the country. Fluctuating rates of exchange, dumping duties and other regulations have been a tremendous barrier to importation, and I doubt if the situation will be clarified much by the terms of this treaty.
The convention to which the minister referred, which was made by the late government on December 15, 1922, was not for any specified time, as has been pointed out. The present government saw fit to terminate that treaty, and their reason was very clear. They pointed out that under the terms of, the treaty there were certain definite rates given France which also applied to other countries enjoying most favoured nation treatment, and that in this case the rates were so low as to be injurious to Canadian production. I have no quarrel with the government on that score; that is their policy, but I doubt very much if the terms of the treaty will bring the relief anticipated or will increase trade to any great extent.
Under the old treaty the French colonies were all included with France. The minister has pointed out that since the old convention was made there have been some changes in the tariff structure of France by which a separate tariff is maintained in what they term the non-assimilated colonies, and the same tariff is maintained in the assimilated colonies. Under the old treaty Canada gave concessions to France with regard to the intermediate tariff and most. favoured nation treatment. As the minister pointed out, on ninety-two items it also gave a ten per cent reduction from the intermediate tariff, and on three items of textiles a fifteen per cent reduction, while on one hundred and thirty-one items there were fixed duties lower than the intermediate rates. In connection with the ninety-two items on which there was a ten per cent reduction from the intermediate tariff and in connection with the three textile items the proportionate differences between the general and intermediate tariffs were to be maintained as at the time the treaty was signed. Canada was not obligated to give France any preferences ac' corded to other parts of the empire, and at that time no foreign country was accorded tariff reductions more favourable than those
specifically granted to France in the treaty.
I notice that the minister has gone further; he has given France the British preferential rate on some items.
By the former convention France granted Canada minimum rates of duty, including the guarantee of most favoured nation treatment, on 141 items or part items, and on a much longer list of items reductions were granted from the general tariff representing various specified percentages of the difference between the general and minimum rates or, if lower, the rates of duty applied to the United States on products of a similar kind. That is to say, we were given the same rates that were accorded the United States. On all other goods we came under the general tariff as it existed before the notable increase made by the decree of March 28, 1921, so long as United States products were exempted from that increase. Then, in the event of the pre-1921 general tariff being withdrawn from the United States, we were given a reduction from the existing general tariff of 25 per cent of the difference between the general and mimimum tariffs. The French colonies, possessions and so on, not having the same tariff as France gave Canada most favoured foreign nation rates, and St. Pierre, Miquelon, the French West Indies and French Guiana accorded minimum tariff treatment on some or all food products. Not all the French colonies had in force duties lower than their general tariffs.
With regard to a great many items in the French tariff the effect of the Franco-Can-adian convention was to give Canada the same rates that applied to the United States, which country, as I think the minister mentioned this morning, under an agreement made in 1910 was accorded the French minimum on about one hundred items. When the French tariff was increased by the 1921 decree, mentioned a moment ago, the United States was exempted from those increases. Until 1927 the goods of the United States entered France under either the minimum rates secured in 1910 or under an intermediate tariff which consisted of the pre-1921 general tariff. On September 6, 1927, the situation changed; a French decree increased duties, both minimum and general, and a new Franco-German treaty went into force. In consequence many intermediate rates-the pre-1921 general tariff 

which applied to Canada and the United States, lapsed, and as a result the United States was placed under the new general tariff with regard to many products. On the items affected Canada was at once granted reductions from the general tariff in pursuance of the Franco-Canadian convention of commerce.

After some Franco-Ameriean negotiations a French decree of November 15, 1927, followed by decrees of March 15, May 12 and June 28, 1928, in the main restored to the United States the intermediate rates previously enjoyed, except that wherever the new minimum tariff exceeded the old intermediate rates, the new minimum rates went into force. Such were the terms of the old agreement. I do not know that there is any need to review the terms of the new treaty, which the minister has so ably explained, before giving the bill second reading. In committee, of course, we will have to study the schedules in order to arrive at what will be the actual effect, but might I point out briefly that article I of the convention now before us provides:
The natural or manufactured products, originating in and coming from Canada, enumerated in schedule A to this agreement, shall enjoy, on their importation into French customs territory, the French minimum tariff, that is to say the most favoured foreign nation treatment.
The minister will agree that there are no fixed rates here, so there is no particular change between this article and the old convention; France can raise her duties at any time. The minister has explained what is meant by the expression "French customs territory." He has pointed out that these words mean that some territories are under the assimilated and others under the non-assimilated rates. Article 2 provides:
The natural or manufactured products, originating in and coming from the French customs territory, enumerated in schedule C to this agreement, shall enjoy, on their importation into Canada, the rates of the Canadian intermediate tariff-
There is not much change there from the old convention; we would have to examine the customs tariff to see where any change occurs. Article 8 states:
The natural or manufactured products, originating in and coming from Canada, enumerated in schedules A and B to this agreement, and the natural or manufactured products originating in and coming from French customs territory, enumerated in schedules C and D to this agreement shall, on their importation into the territory of the other party, enjoy the most favourable rates accorded to any foreign country that may arise from modifications made in the tariff classification-

That means the best rates both ways, as was provided in article 12 of the original treaty, so again there is no change. Article 4 of the present treaty is very much the same as article 14 of the old treaty except that the verbiage has been changed somewhat, though I doubt very much if it has been clarified. Under article 14 of the old treaty we could not import through United States ports but we could export through United States ports. That is the provision contained in article 4, so again there is no change. I believe article 5 of the present treaty is almost the same as article 2 of the old treaty; certain rights are reserved. Perhaps if I read article 2 of the old treaty it would explain to the house the thought behind this item better than it is explained in the new treaty:
The grant of the minimum tariff for the products enumerated in schedule A means the treatment of the most favoured nation as respects such products, but does not entitle Canada to claim the benefit of any preferential advantage which France may grant to her protectorates or the benefit of any tariff resulting from economic agreements which France may enter into with border states, or the benefits of any tariff which France may grant for products the importation of which is designed to facilitate settlements with those countries that were at war with France during the years 1914-18.
That is identically the same thought that is contained in this long article 5. The special terms which France may have with border states, such as the Luxembourg agreement, which my hon. friend knows about, still exist and will not be given Canada under this new agreement. In the last part of article 5 there is a new clause, section (e), which has to do with exchange, and which was not necessary at the time the former agreement was drawn. Article 6 is amazing:
The high contracting parties undertake not to interfere with the course of trade by any prohibitions or restrictions of importation or exportation.
The minister agrees in that undertaking that he will not put an embargo upon French merchandise; but the exceptions are so broad that clause (f) declares:
All necessary measures to face exceptional or abnormal circumstances and to assure the protection of the economic and financial interests of the country. The duration of these measures shall be limited to the duration of the causes of the circumstances which have brought them into effect.
Who is to be judge? I presume the governor in council, and I submit to the minister that he has drafted a treaty which, so far as the agreement not to put on embargoes

or restrictions or prohibitions is concerned, gives him ample power under the clauses that follow to impose all the restrictions he likes. Article 7 is the same as article XVI of the old treaty.
The natural or manufactured products of the territory of either of the high contracting parties," exported to the territories of the other, shall not be subjected to pther or higher duties or charges than those paid on the exportation of similar articles of any other foreign country.
In other words, there shall not be an export tax on goods sold to France any higher than the export tax which is placed on goods sold to any other country. In my opinion, that is more carefully covered in article XVI of the old agreement:
The high contracting parties grant to each other as regards export duties and taxes the most favoured nation treatment. France and Canada grant to each other reciprocally the treatment of nationals as respects the protection of trade marks, patents, commercial names, industrial designs and patterns, names of origin of products and the prevention of unfair competition.
Article 11 of the new agreement makes this provision:
Each of the high contracting parties agrees to protect within its territorial limits the natural or manufactured products of the other party against all forms of dishonest competition, particularly with regard to the use, for commercial purposes, of false indications, relative to the place of origin, nature, kind or substantial qualities of goods.
Each of the high contracting parties agrees to insure within its territorial limits, respect for the appellations of origin of wine. . . .
I submit to the minister that he has gone quite a distance in that clause.

The textiles which we import from France are largely textiles of very high value, not sold in large quantities in this country, and owing to the financial depression of the last two or three years the consumption of that class of goods has been reduced, while undoubtedly, owing to the rescission of the treaty, from June last the imports have been restricted by reason of the fact that instead of our intermediate tariff with a reduction of 10 per cent applying to many of these goods our general tariff has since been applied.

I am very much obliged to the minister for the very interesting and detailed statement he has just submitted. There is one other question on which I would like a little further information, that is the question relating to the minimum tariff. I did not quite catch what the minister said this morning on this question. Do I understand that the present minimum tariff, which Canada receives from France is fixed, or is it liable to be changed at any time by the French government?

The minimum tariff is different on each item. The minimum tariff is liable to change at the option of the French
*Mr. Cahan.]
government at any time, there is no restriction. I show the hon. gentleman my brief on the French minimum tariff concerning Canadian imports. Under each item of that tariff I had prepared a brief for the purpose of negotiations, but it is so large and varied that I am afraid this discussion would be greatly prolonged if we had to go into the details. If this treaty passes this parliament and comes into force I have no doubt the Minister of National Revenue in his department and also particularly the Minister of Trade and Commerce will circulate throughout the country a detailed statement of the duties which are imposed under each item of the French minimum tariff which is of interest to Canada, and also a detailed statement of the French maximum tariff from which certain percentages. are reduced according to these schedules.

The minister stated this
morning that the French maximum tariff was apparently designed to prevent entirely the importation of certain commodities into that country, and that under the minimum tariff fair protection in their market was still provided. He has stated now that there is nothing to prevent the French government from changing that minimum tariff. I take it then that if they desire to exclude from France any of the commodities which are now given the benefit of the minimum tariff they could immediately, without any notice to this country, change the minimum tariff so that it would have the same effect as their maximum tariff and exclude the goods. I suppose that is the fact?

Canada-Franee Trade Agreement
That is true. They sometimes give a short notice, but they are at liberty to change it without notice, and on the other hand we are at liberty to change our tariff in like manner.

They could at any moment entirely abolish any advantage we have under this treaty, but we also have the privilege, without giving them any notice, of making similar changes in the benefits we are giving to them under the treaty?
Yes, that is correct.

I understood the
minister to say that Canadian wheat under this tariff will enjoy in the French market the minimum tariff of any country in the world. Is that correct?

That is correct, with the
exception of the reservation made with regard to the three Danubian states.
Mr. DONNELLY': Then I should like to ask if there is any difference between this and the former agreement. Did not Canada enjoy the minimum tariff under the former agreement with France, with regard to wheat?
Exactly so.

There was a great deal of criticism from hon. gentlemen opposite with regard to that agreement; they said we only enjoyed the minimum tariff and that France was at liberty to raise or lower that tariff at any time. Are there any restrictions in this treaty to prevent France raising or lowering her tariff against our wheat?

Not the slightest, so far as
I know.

So really there is no
difference between this agreement and the previous agreement with regard to the importation of Canadian wheat into France?

Except that under the
former tariff they were at complete liberty to increase the rate, and they did so four times during the life of the treaty. Under the present treaty they are at liberty to raise the tariff still higher, but if they raise it too high it is for us either to reduce the corresponding advantages they receive or to give notice of the rescission of the treaty. Each side is perfectly free with regard to raising or decreasing the tariff rate.
Then I understand that we are in the same position as previously.
Except that in the old treaty there were many items which were fixed so far as Canada was concerned, and this parliament could not increase those duties except in violation of the agreement.

The only difference I
see is that under this agreement we do not enjoy the lowest tariff rates; there are Danubian states which enjoy that lower rate. Under the old agreement negotiated ' by the Liberal party, which was criticized so severely by hon. gentlemen opposite, the Danubian states did not have a lower tariff. Now we see other countries with a lower rate of duty on their wheat entering France than is given us, and that condition did not exist previously.

I should like to ask just
one other question. We have not had time to examine the provisions of the treaty at all, of course, so I should like to ask the minister whether, as a result of the concessions we give to France, those concessions are given automatically to any other countries.
I believe they will be given automatically to twenty-three other countries which enjoy most favoured nation treatment in Canada, by reason of the outstanding agreements with those countries.

Will the minister be good enough to tell us the difference between the old treaty and the present treaty with regard to maple sugar? Under the old treaty we had only the word "sugar," while in this treaty maple sugar and maple syrup are dealt with specifically. Would the minister tell the committee the tariff rate on maple sugar and maple syrup, which come under items 91 and 93, and would the minister inform the committee what were the old rates?

Under the old treaty the rate was the minimum tariff, which was 170 francs per 100 kilos. At the rate of exchange existing at the time this agreement was negotiated-I have not figured it at the rate to-day-that would mean a duty of $3.02 per hundred pounds on sugar.
On any kind of sugar, or just on maple sugar?

Maple sugar goes in exactly as other sugar goes, except that now there is no specific reduction with regard to maple sugar. In the fiscal year 1931 Canada exported to France only 192 pounds of maple sugar valued at $61. During the fiscal year 1927 Canada exported to France 262,682 hundredweight of sugars of all kinds, valued at

Canada-France Trade Agreement
$1,156,115. On inquiry in France I found that maple sugar and maple syrup were hardly known except by friends of those living in Quebec who occasionally, at Christmas and other times, send them samples of maple sugar and maple syrup, and a small quantity of maple syrup was introduced for the purpose of giving a certain taste to tobacco used in the manufacture of cigarettes. Under this agreement maple sugar and maple syrup remain under the minimum tariff.
Will the same rates apply under this new tariff? The minister said the old rate was about 3 cents a pound. Will that be the rate under this new tariff, which specifically mentions mafile sugar?

It will be exactly the same. Under the maximum tariff it would pay twice the duty, and instead of that tariff of S6.04 per hundred pounds the sole concession I could obtain was to have it placed under the minimum tariff, at one-half that rate.

I am not going to direct any questions to the minister but I should like to make one or two general observations with regard to the treaty. In common with other members of the house I realize that the bargain made by the minister is perhaps as good as could be made by any other hon. member under the circumstances. In spite of the remarks of the minister, however, and the valuable services he has given in this connection, I do not see very much difference between the treaty now before the house and the previous treaty with France, which was abrogated not long ago. As a matter of fact it appears to me that the introduction of this treaty at the present time is in itself a vindication of the former treaty, which was denounced by hon. gentlemen opposite mainly, I believe, because of the minimum tariff imposed by France on commodities we exported to that country. Now we find the government coming to parliament with exactly the same provision, and at any time the government of France can increase their tariffs against goods exported by Canada.
Further, Mr. Chairman, I think this treaty indicates that the idea of blasting our way into the markets of the world has proven an absolute failure. The indications are, as this treaty clearly proves, that we have to negotiate and sometimes we cannot negotiate with other people just as we please. Thirdly, in my opinion, the old idea of treaty making is now more or less obsolete. We have before us at the present moment a trade treaty containing many scores of tariff items, and it is fMr. Cahan.]
not really a treaty in that sense of the word because a treaty that can be abrogated at a moment's notice ceases to be such. What the minister said this morning when he introduced the measure is absolutely true, and I subscribe to it, namely, that France was trying to make herself commercially independent of all other nations. That is perfectly obvious to anyone who has attempted to understand the course of France's actions in the past few years. But what France has been doing is precisely what every other nation has been doing or attempting to do in the same period.

Not for the same
reason.

No; it may not be for exactly the same reasons, but the causes are similar. Within the last few years, with the advent of modern machinery, it has become much more easy for all nations to be self contained- much more easy than it has ever been in the past. We can now manufacture our own goods more easily than we did years ago; we can produce crops from our farms much more easily with modern machinery than at any time in the past. The practice of all nations to-day is therefore to export as much as they can. The nations of the world are becoming exporters, so that treaty making in the old sense is now more or less out of date and almost impossible. The things that France needed some years ago she may not need to-day and the things we need to-day we may not need to-morrow; and what applies to France and Canada applies to every other part of the world. At the same time I am in favour of endeavouring, by every means in our power, to foster closer trade relations between Canada and other countries, but I do not believe that we can bring about such relations by having tariff barriers such as now exist in France. Take wheat, for instance; that country has a tariff against that commodity equivalent to 85 cents a bushel, which works out approximately, on the basis of present value, at about 120 per cent. If wheat goes down the percentage will be greater, though of course if it goes up the percentage will be less. There is no telling however when France may increase her tariff on wheat and thus close what might be a potential market to Canada.
Further, I believe that while we are attempting to foster trade between Canada and France or any other part of the world there is no reason why we should not also foster trade between one province in this dominion and the others. Why should we attempt to export wheat to France when we

Canada-F ranee
Trade Agreement
have, or at any rate until recently had, 1,600,000 people drawing relief in Canada? It might be well for us to have Quebec supply our western provinces with the things she produces and have the western provinces supply the east with the products of the west. Naturally we should then be on a more or less self contained basis, and when we had exports in the form of surplus commodities then I would favour the interchange of commodities between nations, because the more of our surplus commodities we sell abroad and the more foreign commodities we bring in in exchange for ours the better it should be for the people of Canada.
In conclusion let me emphasize the fact that the idea of treaty making is of very little benefit in the long run to the people of Canada as it has been carried on in the last few years. We had an example last summer in connection with the imperial trade conferences, and we have before us to-day, though on a smaller scale, a replica of the agreements which we were called upon to consider last fall. Those agreements between Canada and other parts of the empire have not fulfilled expectations, and I do not believe that the agreement now before us will in any way foster trade between this country and France. On the contrary it might ultimately create a feeling which would not be in the best interests of either country.

Item 128 in schedule A deals with woods, in rough logs not squared, with or without bark, of any length, and the minimum tariff is applied to that item. I cannot find anything with regard to planed, squared or manufactured lumber.
What item is the hon. gentleman referring to?
Items 128, 128bis, 129 and 130.

The minimum tariff is granted on wood in rough logs, not squared, with or without bark, and of a certain circumference, or squared or sawn common wood, and also on paving blocks, but it is confined to that. Those products are the only ones with respect to which they were prepared to give us the minimum tariff. These items were discussed one by one, sometimes for days, but that was the entire concession obtained.
Then we are not at liberty to ship manufactured lumber to France?
Yes, under the general tariff.
We used to ship railway sleepers and bridge timber, partly manufactured.
If the hon. gentleman means sawn common lumber, that goes under the minimum tariff.

Sawn lumber, but not manufactured into flooring and other articles. This is the same as we used to ship to Japan. We can ship to Japan squared timber for further manufacture in that country, as well as to the United States, but on planed or manufactured lumber there is a duty.
If it is sawn lumber, I understand it goes under the minimum tariff; if planed or otherwise dressed or manufactured, it would come under 'their maximum tariff.
The expression used in some of the other customs tariff items is, not further manufactured.

I have taken the items of the French tariff, and in that tariff, under 128, the literal translation would be common woods in the rough-that means not planed or otherwise manufactured-and logs not squared, with a certain circumference. Of that we exported from Canada bo France in 1932, 401 metric tons, while the exports, in metric tons, to other countries were: Austria, 38,000; Belgium, 12,000; Finland, 57,000; Germany, 37,000; Latvia, 13,000; Poland, 22,000; Roumania, 11,000; Sweden, 46,000. So on exactly the same basis Canada was not able to obtain in that market a very large sale for either logs or sawn lumber.

Do they come
in under lumber products and take the minimum rates?

They come in exactly the
same as ours, under the minimum tariff.

Will they be
on the same basis as Canada?
On the same basis.
Does that apply to manufactured or unmanufactured lumber.
That manufactured is under their general maximum tariff.

What is meant by the
words "common woods"? Does that differentiate between soft and hard woods?

It excludes such special
woods as mahogany and others which enter into the manufacture of high class furniture.

Canada-France Trade Agreement

Are birch and maple
excluded?
No; I understand that birch, maple and spruce would come in as common woods.
Are we obtaining any special preference under this treaty with regard to wood products?
No.

There is no change? There
is no advantage?

If the hon. gentleman refers to the old treaty which expired in June, we are getting exactly the same terms as before. If he refers to the maximum tariff which has been in effect since last June, we are getting a reduction, I think of one half or even more.

I should like to ask
the minister a question with reference to the regulations which might affect our exports of wheat to France. For some years past certain countries in Europe have enacted regulations whereby anybody exporting wheat would receive a token or certificate which would permit them to import the same quantity of wheat free of duty. Can the minister state whether France has such a regulation in effect at the present time?

The manufacturer of flour
in France who exports flour made out of French wheat can obtain a special licence to import a corresponding quantity of foreign wheat. This is only done by the granting of special licences and it was under such special licences that a very considerable part of our exports of hard wheat in recent years have been imported into France.
That was free of duty?

Upon the export of flour
made from French wheat they can obtain, under certain restrictions, the right to import foreign wheat for mixing purposes. This is imported at a lower rate of duty than the minimum.
Much lower?

My impression is that it
is free of duty or a very low rate.
I think it is ten cents.

Does this treaty limit
us to a quota? Just before one o'clock the minister was giving the details of the importations of wheat into France. I was not in the chamber at the time but these figures have been given to me. The minister also 
recited the rates of tariff which had applied to Canadian wheat and I think he went as far back as when the rate was only fifteen cents per bushel. From that rate it had mounted up until last June the rate was $1.75.
The maximum tariff rate.

Because the treaty was nullified in June, Canadian wheat was subject to a tariff of $1.75 per bushel. As far as Canada was concerned, there was no minimum tariff because we had no treaty. I shall repeat the figures given by the minister and he can correct me if I am wrong. In 1929 we exported
5.000.	000 bushels of "wheat to France for which we received $6,000,000. In 1930 we exported
6.000.	000 bushels for which we received $7,000,000. In 1931 we exported 8,000,000 bushels for which w^e received $7,000,000. In 1932 we exported 20.000,000 for which we received $12,000,000. In 1933 we shipped 15,000,000 bushels.
I have not the quantity for 1933 but the price received was $8,901,000.
The minister does not have the volume which made up that $8,000,000?
No.

The minister told the hon. member for Willow Bunch that under certain conditions when millers in France exported flour made from French wheat they were allowed to import foreign wheat. I do not know whether the minister can tell us but it would be very interesting to know just what percentage of the exports of 1932 and 1933 went in under the minimum tariff and what percentage went in under this other arrangement.
I have no statistics and I do not think they were available during the discussions.
The minister will notice that our exports have been increasing from year to year. I am interested to find out just why that increase has taken place.

There is some difference between the French and Canadian statistics. It was stated during the discussions that the Canadian statistics contained only the quantity of wheat exported direct to France. It was stated that vessels have left Canadian ports with wheat consigned to Liverpool or Southampton and have been diverted to France while on the way. Such wheat would appear in the French but not in the Canadian statistics. Leaving that aside, I might state to the committee that the very best opinion I could form after discussing this matter for five

or six hours a day for many days is that the French have not the slightest intention of allowing wheat to come in from Canada or anywhere else which will interfere with the French domestic production. I think it will be found that in the years when the Canadian exports decreased, the production of French domestic wheat has been increased, and then, when there has been an increase in the Canadian exports, it will be found to be due to a partial failure in the French wheat crop of that year.
I can offer no hope to the committee that France is likely to change this policy.
In spite of the fact that under this treaty we are able to export wheat to France at eighty cents per bushel, the Canadian growers will have no larger market than they had before.

They will have just the
market that is permitted by the French production. When I was there, only three per cent of foreign wheat was allowed to enter into manufacture of flour. Since I left France,
I have seen a later decree that only one per cent of foreign wheat could enter into the manufacture of flour. Therefore our wheat market in France is unstable owing to the policy of that country to restrict by prohibitive measures, for an import of one per cent or three per cent is a restrictive measure, the importation and the use in France of foreign, including Canadian wheat.

I want to thank the
minister for his honest and frank statement concerning the exportation of our wheat to France. I trust this trade agreement which we now have before us has not been the cause of the French government lowering our quota from three to one per cent, as he has just stated to be the case.

Our quota has not been
changed from three to one per cent. I said that while I was in France, the total foreign importation was limited to three per cent. I understand by a decree which I have seen since, the total foreign importation has been limited to one per cent. That percentage may be increased to 5, 10 or 11 per cent if there is a fair prospect that the French crop for the ensuing year is not coming up to the normal standard.

The minister this morning, if I understood him aright, said that there are' some European countries which have treaty arrangements with France whereby they are allowed 30 per cent less than the minimum-
Canada-Franee Trade Agreement

They get a rebate on the
minimum rate. France, under the Stress agreement, if I remember correctly, was to advance certain funds to assist in the rehabilitation of those three Danubian states. France grants to them first the right to export to her 30 per cent of her annual imports of wheat, each state of the three to have the advantage of 10 per cent of France's annual imports, and there is on that importation of wheat a rebate in duty which is. paid back to those three countries for the purpose of assisting certain public works there.
What percentage of the duty paid is returned?

I had the figures before me
this morning, but my memory is 30 per cent.

At the present time
that would foe about twenty-four cents a bushel.
A little more than that.

Is it the practice of the
French government to lower the duty on wheat in years when their own crop is not sufficient for their needs?

In recent years there has
been no lowering of the duty; each change has been an increase of duty. The French farmer is a very potent factor in French politics. When 1 was in Paris I saw a demonstration against the government of the day when, by the numbers I saw in the streets there must have been some thousands who had come in to the city to make certain protests against certain proposals of the French government.
Did they get a hearing?

I saw streets of Paris lined
with police and soldiers for the purpose of maintaining order in that city.
The hon. member for Willow Bunch says that I am frank. I am very frank; I am not holding out to the wheat growers of Canada the hope of getting any very substantial market in France except in those years when the French production is not up to the demands of their domestic consumption.

I do not agree with the minister in the last statement he has made. I think he agrees with me that in some years when the French production of wheat has been high, we have had a fairly good export to that country. I also believe the regulations made from time to time as to rebating to the millers of flour an amount equal _ to the duty paid if the wheat were of foreign

Canada-France Trade Agreement
origin really constitute the factor which enables us to ship wheat to France. If France does a very substantial export business of flour milled from domestic wheat, under some internal arrangements, most of our wheat enters. I cannot understand how Canadian wheat could have entered under the general duty and sold in France at the price at which it was sold there during the past year. The minister knows wheat in France to-day is not as high as wheat in Canada plus the rate of duty which has been charged during the past year.
Yes.
If the prices are higher. I would like to know them.

I figured it up at the rate
of exchange of the day-when domestic wheat was selling at $1.30 per bushel, the price having been reduced in a short time, as alleged by those arguing the case, from $1.75 per bushel, and there was a vigorous protest throughout the country against this reduction in price.

What was the rate of
duty that day?

About eighty-five cents a
bushel minimum and I am told-and this is information that may not be accurate; it is not official-that they were able to buy Canadian wheat and land it at that time, at a French port ait about forty to forty-five cents a bushel.

Was eighty-five cents the
general rate at that time?

It was the minimum tariff
rate.
Were we getting the minimum tariff rate at that time?

No; we had not since the
previous June.

What rate of duty was
Canadian wheat paying at that time?
It was $1.75.
That is the point.
It would be impossible to land Canadian wheat in France during the past year at forty-one cents a bushel.

It was said to be between
forty cents and fifty cents.

I may not have expressed myself well. At the very time of which the minister speaks, when Canadian

wheat was paying a duty of $1.75, when sold in France. Even if the cost of the wheat was only fifty cents a bushel, with the duty it would cost $2.25 delivered in France.

The hon. gentleman means
that a rebate was being given at that time?
Yes.

A rebate was being given
which brought the duty down to the present minimum tariff.

That is the point I am making; the effect of the rebate permitted the gale of our wheat. Therefore I contend that if whatever wheat we have sold was by virtue of the rebate, the minister is not quite correct in saying that in future our sales of wheat to France will be governed entirely by the scarcity of production within her territory. I believe our sales to France will continue to be governed, as in the past, by the effect of the rebate on flour exported.
Will flour exported displace our wheat in other markets?

Flour exported makes
an opportunity for us to ship in wheat.

That is to France, but
flour exported to other countries takes the place of our flour or wheat.

It might do so or it
might take the place of the softer varieties of United States wheat.

How much wheat does
France consume in a year?
I have not the particulars of the production. She is one of the largest wheat producing countries of Europe.
I said consumption.
That can be found from the imports and what She produces; I have not the figures.

What is the minimum
tariff regarding item 37, butter, fresh, melted or salted?

Item 37 of the French tariff is "butter, fresh, melted or salted," the minimum tariff being 200 francs per 100 kilos which, at the time of negotiating-and I have the figures here-amounted in Canadian currency to $3.55 per hundred pounds or a little over cents a pound. At the same fime the general tariff was $7.11 per 100 pounds, but there was put into force for one year-from September 28, 1932, while these discussions were going on-a higher duty for a period of

one year for the protection of French production, and that higher duty amounted to 700 francs per 100 kilos, S12.44 cor 100 pounds, or nearly 124 cents a pound. That duty will be in effect until September 28, 1933, unless previously repealed by decree of the French government.

I ask the minister to turn to items 46 to 49 inclusive, appearing in Schedule A. Item 46 is for "fish, dried, salted or smoked." Will the minister tell me whether there is any regulation in force in France, and if so what, providing a bonus to salt water fishermen?

I presume the hon. member refers to the St. Pierre fishermen. I cannot answer the question accurately, but I know that the minimum tariff rate is high, and I understood that that was so for the protection of French fishermen fishing off the St. Pierre, Miquelon and Newfoundland coasts. When I was dealing with the French government the minimum tariff ran, on different kinds of dried, salted and smoked fish, from 100 francs to 300 francs per 100 kilos. That is, there was a tariff varying from $2.67 per 100 pounds to $5.33 per 100 pounds according to the class of fish. On dried and certain other kinds of fish, which they call stock fish, salted or smoked, the tariff was $1.78 for 100 pounds.
Is cod classified separately?
Dried, salted or smoked cod is under the first classification.
That is, from $2.67 to $5.33 per 100 pounds.
Yes.
The minimum tariff is the same under the old treaty as under the new. It applies in both cases.
Yes.

The minister referred to lobsters, under item 49. I am a little apprehensive about the note annexed to Schedule A which has to do with the importation of lobsters, and which seems to forecast the possibility of a quota regulation. Could the minister tell us anything on that point?
There is a quota. To which pages did you refer?
Pages 14 and 15 of the bill. On page 15 there is a reference to lobsters.

Yes, there is a quota on lobsters going into France. Our quota for the minimum tariff is 3,000 quintals or 660,000 odd pounds. We are not prevented from sending an amount in excess of that quota, but we have to pay the maximum tariff duty on the excess.
I did not understand that the quota is actually in force.
Yes, they have a regular quota system.

I notice that the second paragraph on page 16 reads:
In case the importation into France of canned lobsters and spiny lobsters is submitted to quotas, the French government reserves the right to submit the importation of the above category originating in Canada to the regime of licences of importation which may he applied to similar goods from other sources.
I took that paragraph to mean that it was possibly envisaged that there would be a quota. The hon. minister states that there is one now.

Certainly a quota was imposed upon us, in view of the fact that under arrangements outstanding 3,000 quintals was the full amount that could be allowed to us at the time. In the previous year we had exported to France 382 metric tons of lobsters preserved or prepared. The imports of France of preserved or prepared lobsters amounted to 6,192 metric tons. Of that amount 2,779 came from Great Britain, 1,170 from Germany, 811 from Japan, 547 from the Union of South Africa, 382 from Canada, 152 from a French colony, and 129 from Soviet Russia.
Over half came from Canada.
No; the United Kingdom sent more than we did. Canada sent only 382 metric tons, whereas Japan sent 811. Those figures deal with the year before the rescission of the French treaty.
I believe the minister will find that those lobsters sent from Great Britain to France came originally from Canada.
That may be so.
I think it is. I do not mean that they were all Canadian lobsters, but I suggest that a very large proportion of them were.

As a matter of fact it would not make any difference whether or not the shipment was direct because, with respect to

Canada-France Trade Agreement
lobsters, I understand Great Britain enjoys the French minimum tariff. So that whether they were shipped from Canada direct or shipped via Southampton or Liverpool they would receive exactly the same treatment, namely the minimum tariff, in France.
Has Great Britain enjoyed a minimum tariff under a treaty arrangement?

I believe Great Britain enjoys a minimum tariff in France on almost everything, in view of the fact that up until last year French productions were admitted into England at the lowest possible rates of duty. I cannot speak for the last two or three months.
I am wondering whether or not England and France even had the formality of a treaty.
Oh, yes, there is a treaty outstanding.

I believe the minister stated that 382 metric tons were shipped by Canada to France. Then I did not quite oatch the figures that he gave as those which would be applicable to Canada. I thought it was more than that.
No, it is three thousand quintals at 220 pounds and a fraction.

That is 660,000 pounds.
Now if a metric ton-here is where the minister has me completely at a disadvantage as he has been dealing with metric measures -if a metric ton is the same as our ton, that is 2.000 pounds, then 382 tons would be 764,000 pounds, whereas the quota, he is pointing out, is only 660,000, indicating that the quota could not have been in effect at that time, if I am right in my figures.

I cannot tell as to the quota being in effect. As far as my memory goes, at the time of our discussion there was a temporary quota in effect with regard to importation of canned and preserved lobsters into that country.
Coming back to cod, which is a very important product of the lower St. Lawrence, has any real advantage been secured on the French market for salted cod?

No, it remains under the
minimum tariff as it was before.

In reference to cod,
would my hon. friend tell me the amount of dry salt cod which the figures show was imported into France from Canada, referring to items 45 and 46.

I can simply give the total
import into France of cod; dried, salted and smoked; which was 5,069 metric tons. That is for the year 1930, the last figures I have.
That is the total imports?

Yes. These are French
figures. The Minister of Trade and Commerce, who has the figures at hand, tells me that our exports of dried cod to France were practically nothing in recent years.

They could not be, over
that tariff wall. They are paying the fishermen 75 cents to $1 per hundredweight, and the minister is pointing out that the minimum tariff is $5 and $6. So I cannot see how there could be much. With regard to exports of fresh fish from Canada to France, can the minister tell me if the figures show any appreciable amount?
Yes, $40,000 last year.
Will the minister tell me the minimum tariff on fresh fish, that is item 46?

It is about $1.33 of our
money per hundredweight. I am computing at the rate of exchange as at the time of the negotiations. It has fluctuated somewhat.

One wonders whether
there really is any advantage at all in putting items like this in the treaty. I quite understand this was in the previous treaty, but in view of the height of the minimum tariff can the minister tell me if there was any discussion about the possibility of dropping it altogether? What is the advantage of including it?
