maintopic: CANADA-FRANCE CONVENTION CONCERNING RIGHTS OP NATIONALS AND COMMERCIAL AND SHIPPING MATTERS
CANADA-FRANCE CONVENTION CONCERNING RIGHTS OP NATIONALS AND COMMERCIAL AND SHIPPING MATTERS
speechtext:
While this convention, may be terminated by either party upon six months' notice, it is of such character that its provisions will likely be maintained for an indefinite period of time, affording a substantially permanent settlement of the problems with which it is directly concerned. Obviously it would have been unsatisfactory to incorporate the provisions dealing with the rights of Canadian nationals, Canadian corporate enterprises and Canadian shipping in a provisional trade arrangement which may be revised at the close of a period of one year.
The present convention concerning the rights of nationals and commercial and shipping matters deals solely with the second class of commercial relations. It defines and determines the legal rights and privileges of. Canadian nationals in France and in the French colonies, protectorates and mandated territories and in corresponding manner the reciprocal rights and privileges of French nationals in Canada. It defines and determines the rights and privileges of Canadian corporate enterprises doing business in France and in territories under French rule, and in corresponding manner it deals with the rights and privileges of French corporate enterprises in Canada. Similarly, and on a reciprocal basis, it provides for Canadian shipping in the ports of French territories and French shipping in Canadian maritime ports.
The present convention follows closely the precedent generally adopted for dealing with similar problems and modern commercial treaty practice. It accords the Canadian nationals and Canadian business and shipping interests in French territories, as a matter of right, as favourable a position as has been established in modern treaty practice between countries which have reached the same advanced stage of civilization as these two countries. It should be observed that it also includes the undertaking by the two governments to deal with the special problems of corporate taxation which have given rise to difficulties in recent years.
In article 2 of this convention Canada and France agree to conclude another convention with regard to the subject of double taxation of persons and companies engaged in business in both countries. We discussed that third convention as it was a matter of special importance to Canadian banks and corporations which are doing business in France by branches or agencies. There has been a very considerable and insistent demand that Canada should negotiate with France with regard to an equitable adjustment of these matters. At Paris we

drew up such a convention, which has since been approved by the officials of the Department of National Revenue here and which is now under the consideration of the financial and fiscal experts of the French government. As however their approval had not been obtained by May 12, it was inevitable that there should be a delay; but we hope at the next approaching session of parliament to submit to this parliament this third convention dealing with that particular subject of double taxation.
This convention, in terms, does not infringe on the immigration laws of either country. It gives to the nationals of either country the right to acquire property interests in the other country. The nationals of each country are exempted from compulsory military service in the other. The nationals of either country are granted free access to the courts of justice, either as plaintiffs or as defendants, in all processes within the jurisdictional authority of the courts of the respective countries, and merchants and manufacturers of either country are entitled not only to travel in the other country but to bring in samples for the purpose of trading and soliciting orders, and companies and societies are authorized to establish branches and carry on business in each of the countries concerned.
Provision is made in article 8, which is perhaps an innovation, whereby Canada reserves to itself the right to appoint consuls general, consuls, vice-consuls and consular agents, to reside in the ports and towns of French territories. With regard to the shipping of goods over the railways of either country, article 9 provides that goods shipped through the territory of one of the high contracting parties, with destination in the territory of the other party, on the railways of the latter, in relation to conditions and costs of transportation, and to rates and taxes of every description affecting transportation, shall receive as favourable treatment as that which is generally applicable to similar goods in the interior traffic of that country, under the same conditions, for the same directions and for the same distances, and shall enjoy most favoured nation treatment. With regard to the right of transshipment across either country, the goods shipped through a country are entitled to most favoured nation treatment and to the same treatment as that given to the transport of domestic goods and commodities. Article 13 contains a provision with regard to the rights of the shipping of one country which enter the ports of the other. There is also a provision covering vessels entering for shelter

Convention with France
and those that may be stranded or wrecked. Article 20 reads:
If a dispute arises between the high contracting parties in regard to _ the proper interpretation or application of this convention which cannot be solved by diplomatic means, the matters in dispute shall be submitted to the Permanent Court of International Justice at the Hague.
In dealing with the provisions with regard to the rights of French shipping generally and of wrecked and stranded ships, I took particular pains to keep in mind the existing Can-adion law dealing with these -matters and I think I can assure bon. gentlemen that the provisions of this treaty are entirely consistent with the law at present in existence in Canada. In dealing with Canadian shipping, for the purposes of this convention we confined it to shipping registered in Canada. I might have proceeded further and perhaps a little more definitely but at the time of the negotiations we knew that the shipping laws of the British commonwealth were being revised and that at an early date Canada must recast and reenact her own shipping law in compliance with the resolutions of the imperial conference. I sought to avoid any distinct engagement in this convention which was not thoroughly consistent with our existing statutes and with the policy which hon. gentlemen opposite inaugurated at London and which this government has consistently carried into effect so far as we have dealt with shipping matters. I commend this bill to the consideration of the committee.

speechtext: As I understand the Secretary of State, he proceeded in this matter in the manner agreed to at the imperial conference of 1923 with respect to the negotiation of treaties. So far as the department is concerned, there has been no difference in the instructions given to our graders, nor has there been any difference in the operations of the graders themselves. In Denmark they have one considerable advantage over us in the grading of hogs in that the entire kill is graded on the rail. We have given a good deal of effort to seeing whether we cannot in Canada also work out some system whereby hogs can be graded on the rail. One of the greatest difficulties has been overcome, that of identity. Different means of maintaining the identity of the hog, 53719-318
from the time it left the farmyard until it reached the slaughter house, had been tried-branding with indelible ink and so on-but such methods were not satisfactory. However, we have at last devised a method that should leave grading very little subject to error in maintaining the identity of the hog as shipped from farm to slaughter house. But the farmer who ships his hogs and sells them on the basis of grading on the rail will have to wait for final payment until the animal has been slaughtered. To illustrate with an extreme case, there are a great number of hogs that are shipped from western Canada, in particular from Edmonton, as far east as Moncton, New Brunswick. Coming through Moncton last fall I was surprised to learn that live hogs had been shipped to that point from Edmonton. I admit that that is an extreme case but I am sure that the farmers would hesitate quite a while before being in favour of waiting that long for their returns. There would be another difficulty which would confront us before we could adopt the policy of grading on rail. Some of the biggest losses in the packing of hogs are caused by bruises or injuries en route. When strange groups of hogs are put with other strange groups they are liable to fight with each other and the teeth and hoof marks make bruises which prevent the bacon being put in the top class. A farmer might have ten select hogs which because of bruises in shipment, either by truck or rail, would not grade as select. A peculiar thing is that hogs shipped by truck are more liable to bruises than those shipped in car lots. If the car lot shipment takes two or three days en route to market the hoof and tooth marks may almost entirely disappear, and they do sometimes disappear entirely as far as leaving any marks on the slaughtered animal is concerned. We realize that grading on rail is a much more accurate method of grading but we have some difficulties yet to overcome.

After having been told in the agriculture committee how the poor old cow has been exploited I have decided that I have been at the wrong end of the cow all these years. If I had been handling milk, probably I would have made as much as a friend from Montreal made. I sold him a few cows once and it was hard work to pay for them, but I heard him tell that committee that his plant is worth over $2,000,000. I know I did a great deal more work for the farmers than he ever did, but I did not get that much for it. I am anxious for the success of the live stock industry; I do not want it to fail, but if you do not go at it in a practical way it will be a failure all the way through. You can get a lesson from a practical Scotchman just west of here. I did not know he was a Scotchman until I asked him; no wonder it is a success. He has 250 of the best white face cattle I have ever looked at. My hon. friend from North Battleford was there, addressed the meeting and then went out in the field with this gentleman and' looked over his herd of cattle. Go to the stock yards and get a few practical men and forget about cooperation. Cooperation is only exploitation; that is what it has been in eveiy market. The farmer has been fooled; they have got him to ship his cattle through that one channel while some fellow draws a big salary and keeps a good fat position for himself.
In this connection, Mr. Chairman, I remember listening to one of the best broadcasts I ever heard with regard to these cooperative schemes we are talking about. This broadcast was by Bob Schuler, an evangelist in Los Angeles, who said, "Labour, you have a perfect right to be organized so long as some man at your head is not leading you for some specific purpose, to get a job in parliament or something else. Farmers, you are the biggest fools that ever went into organization." That is what he said over the radio, and he went on to say, "I am one of you; I have ten acres of walnuts just outside Los

Angeles, and my wife and I shook hands every year when we sold the walnuts, for which we received $1,600. Then a nice, clever young man, with one of these baby moustaches, came to the door and said we should join up in order to help our brethren get better organization. I went into the organization, and I have never Shaken hands with my wife since. I get $400 a year for my walnuts now; that young man gets $30,000 a year and he does not know walnuts from hickory nuts."
How about your grain pool in the west, which you asked me to help get through? I worked hard to put over that idea, thinking it was a good thing, but what a farce it has turned out to be. Some of the men have not been paid for their 1028 crop yet. The farmers are being drawn into some fool scheme all the time. Leave the markets the way we had them in the old days; throw them open. The Minister of Agriculture can do it by a stroke of the pen. You do not want these close restrictions, surrounded by all kinds of fool policies. Who owns the stock yards in Canada, with the exception of a few privately owned yards in the west, which should be under strict supervision. I would have all the live stock shipped to the stock yards; I would not let them go direct to the packers. At present a truck driver will pick up a farmer's hogs out in the country and take them right to the yard of the packer. What will happen the poor farmer? If you knew some of the packers as well as I know them you would say the farmer would not get any the best of it. Who owns one of the stock yards in Winnipeg? It is owned by the three railroads. We own the Canadian National and the Canadian Northern, and that leaves the Canadian Pacific with only a minority say. The government controls -the majority of the stock in that yard, so why does not the minister throw it open and give us back the system we had in the old days? You could go to -the hay market then and bring back a load of hay for your cattle, but now what do you get? You buy a bale of hay weighing eighty pounds but you pay for a hundred pounds. They ask you to bale it at eighty pounds so it will be easy to lift, but when the poor farmer comes to buy it he pays for a hundred pounds. Look at the bills; they are appalling in comparison with what it cost years ago. It is no wonder the live stock industry is dwindling into insignificance; a man has no chance.
Let -me say here, Mr. Chairman, that unless the railroads put back the freight rates to the level of forty yeans ago, and reduce them by

forty per cent, no man will be able to farm successfully in western Canada, particularly in regard to live stock. When the road was coupled up at Jackfish in 1885 they said to us, "Give us fourteen -cars o-f cattle and we will give you a trainload rate." There was a crew of five on that train and we paid 60J cents a hundred from Winnipeg to Montreal. Today a train consists of seventy-five cars of cattle, but the crew still numbers only five, and the railway companies charge up the increased cost to labour, though it is not labour. They are paying the men a little more money, but they are not -being paid too much. The late James Hill went out through Montana and the Dakotas to make a survey of what was wrong with the farmers in order to see why they were going bankrupt and leaving the land. He came home and cut freight rates in half.
Hon. gentlemen opposite harp about the tariff. They remind me of a Chinese concert I heard in Vancouver; it was played all on one string. Why not be big enough and broad enough to help save the country and the farmers? Why not help meet the situation that exists to-day? The old ship is floundering around in the trough of the sea; why not help guide it safely through? Why play politics all the time? I am surprised at my hon. friend from South Battleford; I never thought he would leave himself wide open by referring to that man Serkau, who has done nothing but exploit the farmers of the west. The Toronto Star fell for it; the headlines said Mr. Bennett should resign. I wonder if hon. gentlemen opposite are big enough now to say that Mr. Bennett was right, if they are broadminded enough to say, "You were right about this man. He had his hands in the treasury of Manitoba and you stopped him from getting hold of the funds in Ottawa." I am proud .that the Prime Minister did that, and I am sorry that my hon. friend from South Battleford should get up and introduce the subject of shipping cattle to Russia under the Serkau scheme. Unless we wake up and do something right now to bring about an improvement in our pure bred sires and to distribute them throughout the country we are going to be faced with very serious competition from Russia, because representatives of that country are in Scotland right now buying all the pure bred sires they can get hold of. They are going -to take those sires back and we are going to face strong competition from them. Let us build up our herds; let us buy more pure breds and distribute them among the farmers so that we can build up the live stock industry of Canada.

Supply-Agriculture-Live Stock
Don't let Russia beat us to it. I assure you, it would be impossible to sell anything but top cattle to the Russians; they know what they are about. I saw some of them in Perth, Scotland, once buying pure breds and 1 would hate to see them come to this country, if that were possible, and take the tops of our cattle, leaving us with the culls. Heaven knows we have enough culls at the present time without getting more. I want us to breed a better grade of cattle in this country. Serkau came to me and made this remark, "You are not too old to go back into business?" I replied, "I don't think I am. What do you mean?" Then he asked me whether I would join him and I said, "No, do you think I would go to the Minister of Trade and Commerce with such a scheme as that? Do you think I would go to the Prime Minister with such a scheme? Why, he would throw me out of his office and he would be justified."
After reading about those cows that came here with Champlain, and having heard how they were exploited, I felt that I ought to say something, and I could not keep still after my hon. friend from South Battleford broke in. I thought I would let him know all about Mr. Serkau.

Our good friend from Marquette has on previous occasions read me a similar lecture on the live stock industry.
I was interested when he suggested that we could not ship cattle to Russia because of the twenty-two day voyage, because I can remember the time when we made a shipment, though a limited one, that took many more days than that in crossing. The hon. gentleman knows his Bible well enough to answer this question: How did Noah manage to keep his cattle all that time on the ark? I think he will agree that we can ship cattle much more easily than horses, and we have shipped horses to Russia on more than one occasion. So that the objection from the point of view of the voyage is not well founded. Let me tell my hon. friend that I am not through with the cattle industry yet, for it happens that I am not as old as he, and naturally I am looking to a somewhat longer future in the business. I can assure him that my interest in the farmer and in the cattle breeder is as great as his own, and it was because of that interest I have in them that I wanted us to ship 100,000 head of cattle. I wanted that done in the interests of the cattle producers. As late as 1921 we were able to ship to the United States five times that number in one year, whereas last year we shipped only 18.000. We have shipped
a few cattle to the old country, but what the industry needs to-day, as proved by the record that was tabled in the house, is a wider market. We need more markets. My chief reason for getting up to-night was to give the minister, and the Prime Minister as well, an opportunity to tell the country why that attitude was taken with regard to the Serkau deal. So far as Serkau is concerned, I knew nothing about him. My hon. friend from Marquette told me privately what he has told the house to-night and through the house the country; he was the one that made me acquainted with the facts. There is nothing in this document tabled in the house that would indicate to me that what he has read to-night is true. In Mr. McDonald especially Mr. Serkau had a real business man who knew the cattle business probably as well as my hon. friend from Marquette.

I admit that we did ship a good many cattle to the United States, but I would ask all practical men in this house this question. What man among them, if it were not for some political reason, would ship a well-bred growing yearling out of the country to be processed in the United States? Certainly I would not do it. If I had a well-bred yearling on my farm I do not think the United States would get it. I have seen calves leaving Winnipeg on their way to the United States, trainloads of cattle starved for two days until they got on the scales under 1,000 pounds. Our cattle industry has been ruined by inexperienced men who have got into the business. We shipped to the United States in 1930, just when this government was coming into office, 35,000 yearlings, well-bred animals; also trainloads of calves leaving the ranches to find their way to Minneapolis. Would not that spell disaster to the cattle trade? Surely any practical man knows that this sort of thing was the ruination of the industry. Some poor chap found himself under the necessity of going to the barn and taking out a yearling which he had to sacrifice for binder twine. My sympathy goes out to that man. That is the type of man I want to help become successful so that he will not have to make such sacrifices. Let me point out that that is not the logical market for yearlings. They do not want your 1,000 pound cattle; they want small cattle. Personally I do not care Where they go after they have passed that weight.
Now, what is the use of fitting up ships to take cattle overseas when with a change of government a high duty is imposed upon them? It simply means the disruption of the

Supply-Agriculture-Live Stock
trade. We were sending constant shipments of cattle to the British market, and receiving in western Canada splendid returns, but a restriction was put on on the other side with the result that our trade was disrupted-the most important industry in the west. I do not regard it as second to wheat, because you cannot grow wheat unless you fertilize the land and you cannot fertilize it without cattle. But I emphasize the fact that the shipping of young cattle is absolutely wrong. I want to see a channel opened up to the British market; I want to see ships fitted up so that our cattle men can obtain a market, shipping their cattle at reasonable rates. More than that, I want to see the railways, which are giving cheap rates to passengers, extend cheap rates to the cattle industry. You can keep UP tlie price of wheat; I am not as much interested in that as in cattle, because eventually you will grow more wheat and have better crops by keeping a good stock of cattle on the farm.
Mr. SPEAIiMAN: Has the minister still in mind the possibility of creating a marketing board at some time? In the part of Canada with which I am familiar, and throughout eastern Canada as well, the farmers' organizations and farmers generally are still very desirous of seeing such a body created. While they do not look to the board to perform miracles, they do look to it as offering the means of bringing some order out of the chaos which now exists in marketing conditions. I hope the minister has not given up the idea.
Let the farmer alone; he is as good a salesman as anybody.

I understand that this company in Winnipeg approached the government to ask for financial backing or a financial guarantee before they made these shipments to Russia or before the deal with Russia was completed. I understand also that when their suggestion was turned down, some little time afterwards they agreed to go on with the deal without any financial guarantee; all they wanted was an assurance of what the regulations would be in the future. I was told by one of the officials of a well known oil company that they had approached the government in connection with this matter. They were willing to finance the deal, buy the cattle and take Russian oil in exchange provided the government would assure them that the regulations would not be changed. They could not get this assurance and for that reason the deal was not put through. I was told this by two officials in the oil company and I should 
like to know the reason why this assurance was not given to Mr. Serkau and the oil company. The same thing happened in connection with the importation of gasoline from Roumania. We found that gasoline could be laid down at Montreal for six cents a gallon but we could not get any assurance from the government as to what the rate of duty would be or whether any dumping duty would be applied. Can the minister give us any reason why this assurance was not given to either one of these companies?

As far as I am
aware, no such proposition was put up to the government by any oil company. However, granting that it had been put up in the manner the hon. member for Willow Bunch suggests it was, I think, had he been in the place of any member of the government he would have had no hesitation in stating that no government could give an assurance as to what the tariff on any commodity would be in the future. If the government did that for any company or for any individual they would be establishing a precedent and would have to act similarly in the case of all such requests. This would tie the hands of government absolutely.
A very excellent precedent.

Early in
December of last year the press of southern Alberta carried a dispatch stating that a shipment of seventeen carloads of poultry was then between Montreal and Moncton to be shipped to the London market from Saint John. Has the minister any information as to the extent of the poultry shipments last Christmas from Canada to the United Kingdom? Did these Shipments have any beneficial effect upon the local market by eliminating surplus stock, and did the producer in Canada obtain a higher price because of these shipments? What are the prospects for increasing our poultry trade in Great Britain and what percentage of that market can Canada supply? Did we receive any benefits under the Ottawa agreements as far as poultry shipments to Great Britain are concerned?

In November of
last year the Canadian poultry pool investigated the possibility of obtaining wider markets for poultry. Inquiries were made in the United Kingdom but replies were received to the effect that there was no market there, that the market was glutted. In spite of this information they decided to make a trial shipment. The first- shipment was collected

Supply-Agriculture-Live Stock
in Manitoba from four points just outside of Winnipeg. A number of carloads were got together. Great care was exercised in the method in which this poultry was prepared and shipped and careful records were kept of the temperatures of the shipment when en route both by ship and by rail. An effort was made to determine the best possible manner of making future shipments should this trial shipment prove satisfactory. The Department of Agriculture in cooperation with the Department of Trade and Commerce sent Mr. Brown, the chief of the poultry division along with this shipment. Elaborate and carefully prepared publicity was sent along with Mr. Brown and preparations were made to put our poultry before the public of the United Kingdom in the best possible way. I believe there were thirty-three carloads approximating one million pounds of poultry shipped. This shipment received a very fine reception, exceeding all expectations. The poultry sold in the United Kingdom for prices that return to the producer in Canada from three to four cents per pound more than the domestic price at Winnipeg. No one can say what would have happened to the domestic market had this shipment not been made. Inquiries have already been received for from two to three times as much poultry as we Shipped last year. I want to take this opportunity to express before this committee my personal appreciation of the vision and foresight of the president of the Canadian Cooperative Poultry Pool in undertaking this trial shipment in spite of all discouragement. Other companies were appointed but declined to participate. When I say that the price received returned three cents per pound more than the domestic price it must not be forgotten that the depreciation in their currency at that time reduced the price of our product by from five to six cents per pound. In the case of Shipments this year, the increased value of the pound together with the operations of the stabilization fund will mean a further advantage in price. No person can make an estimate of the amount of poultry that the United Kingdom market can absorb, but there is certainly a prospective demand for Canadian poultry. Under the Ottawa agreements we received a ten per cent preference.
Did those shippers of poultry know what the rate of duty would be before they shipped?
There was no duty into the old country.
They knew that?
They did know it. There was a preference of ten per cent applying to shipments made after November 15.

The point I am making is
that they knew what they would have to pay in the form of duty.

They had no assurance
that it would not be raised.
There was no duty. Mr. YOUNG: They knew it?

I understand that some discussion took place in the agriculture committee of the Senate in regard to stock yard charges to farmers. I happen to be a shareholder in a stock yard which I think I can say I was more or less responsible for developing in my own city. It is controlled in Toronto by a bunch of financial racketeers and I know they took thousands of dollars out of the earnings of that yard and developed and extended it further. If my memory serves me aright, last year I received a dividend of 16 per cent, which is not bad. We shareholders can get no infomation. I wrote to the secretary on April 24 asking him for a financial statement and some other questions and he replied on May 12 saying that he had turned my letter over to the president. The president moved1 the office of the company from a downtown office to his own at the stock yards at Toronto and I presume to-day the stock yard at Saskatoon is probably paying a large portion of the rent of his office, stenographer's fees, and so forth, at the stock yard at Toronto. He soaks the Saskatoon stock yard a large sum as president although he has nothing whatever to do; then the other directors of the company who live at Toronto also soak the yard large sums of money. I should like to suggest to the minister that it might be good business in the interests of - stock raisers to hold an investigation into these stock yard charges.

May I ask the minister, if I am in order in doing so on this item, whether he has any reasons to give me why a tubercular tested area has not been established in the county of Saguenay? I spoke to the minister about this matter last year. It was decided to open up such a zone in the counties of Charlevoix, Saguenay, Rober-val and Chicoutimi, and I was told that zones were established in those districts with the exception of the county of Saguenay.

I am not sure
whether I caught the hon. member's question

correctly, but there is part of Saguenay county that is not included in the restricted area.
Why was it not includued?

No application was made for it. The application is made by the municipalities or, I believe in Quebec, by the parishes through the provincial government, but for part of Saguenay county no application was made.

I am sorry I have to disagree with the minister because I think this area was established1 in 1930. Requests and petitions were signed by the municipalities and the farmers' clubs and sponsored by the provincial government at the same time as similar requests were made on behalf of the people in Chicoutimi and Roberval. I think at the same time as the matter was taken up by the hon. member for Chicoutimi I joined with him in signing the petitions and presenting them to the Department of Agriculture.
I think one of the reasons given to me last year or the year before was that there were not enough men on the staff of the Department of Agriculture to look after this matter in the late spring and the fall, but it would be attended to as soon as it would be possible to do so. The minister may have confused the matter, because that is one of the answers he gave to me before; he told me that as soon as men were available to attend to the tests he would see to it that the tests were made.

As I stated, I did
not hear the hon. member's question very clearly in the beginning; I thought he was asking why part of Saguenay county was not included. Part of that county was not included because no request came from it. The other parts of the county were included at that time, and no doubt it is this area to *which the hon. member has reference. Every effort will be made to carry on the work in that particular district. We are taking every step possible, I may say-and I am sure this will be appreciated fully by the hon. member to get as many French speaking veterinaries as are available to do the work not only there but in all parts of Quebec where there are French speaking people.
Has the minister at the present time French speaking veterinaries to attend to this work?

We have a number, but not sufficient to do all the work that there is in Quebec.

Can the minister give the committee any information with respect to the Beatty live stock scheme? I do not know whether it has any connection with the Department of Agriculture, but it received a good deal of advertising when it came into operation a year or so ago.

That is in no way
connected with the Department of Agriculture and I am not in a position to give information concerning it.

Can the minister give a report on the development of the pure bred sire plan which I think he inaugurated himself? It was a plan by which clubs were to be organized in districts throughout the country and when a number organized a club, they were to share a pure bred sire.

The pure bred sire area policy is a provincial one. The hon. member for Bow River, however, means, I believe, the pure bred sire policy inaugurated by me as head of this department. We have up to the end of March, 1933, some 1,280 pure bred sires, chiefly in districts where it is very difficult for the farmer to get high quality sires. I know of nothing that is more appreciated at the present time by the farmers than that policy. Because of their financial condition it is very difficult, if not impossible for many men who appreciate the value of live stock, especially a soldier settler who is starting in, to purchase such animals, and they value the assistance we have given them. One regrettable feature of the matter, however, is that we have not been able to fill the applications for one strain of sires that is in greatest demand; there are not sufficient animals of the right quality in the country.
Was this policy inaugurated recently by the minister or his department?
In the fall of 1930.
How many districts in Quebec, for instance, have taken advantage of this policy so far?

We have not the exact number, but a large number of bulls have gone into the province of Quebec. In addition, in that province we have another policy that is particularly suited to it. In conjunction with the provincial government we pay a grant of 50 per cent for young bulls of sufficiently

Would the
minister, before this part of the subject is disposed of, give us exactly the number of districts served in each of the provinces?

We have not that exact information here. I 'believe they are very well distributed throughout the whole dominion. Under this policy there are more animals available proportionately in the west than in the east, because in the east we have supplementary policies such as the one I have described for the benefit of the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay.
Can the minister give me the figures for Saskatchewan and Alberta?
I have not that information.
Can the minister get it ?
Yes, and I shall be glad to give it to the hon. member.

I wonder if
the minister thinks a man is an agitator who protests against relief which provides him and his family with meals at the rate of five cents apiece. Would the minister not agitate under those conditions? I do not think I have ever been so disgusted in this house in twelve years as I have been to-night when I heard the minister rail at these unfortunate people because they are protesting against such a miserable pittance which does not provide them with enough to keep healthy. I ask the minister to go in person into the homes of these people, study the faces of the children, see the pallor of their countenances due to under-nourishment, and ask himself if he does not think that an officer with wealth who applies for a pension is not a more vicious type of agitator than the man who strives to secure a little better than five cents a meal for himself and his children.
The minister says that the basis upon which this relief is granted is that it is sufficient for civilians. I protest that civilian relief is not adequate, has not been adequate since the beginning of this depression; but to put a soldier on that same basis is gross injustice and inhumanity. The civilian at least has physical fitness, was not subject to the Shocks of war. Here is a case I have under my hand, a man suffering from a gunshot wound in the spine and osteo-myelitis of the left ilium and chronic neurasthenia. Does the minister say that that man is not suffering more than a civilian and is entitled only to the same relief? This condition is intolerable. I do not blame these men for writing letters to this house protesting against such a condition; they would not be Canadians if they did not. It is a wonder to me that they have been so unutterably patient up to this time.
I have listened to what the hon. member for Bow River has said, and I think he is speaking largely of item 198 rather than item 206.
I am speaking to the point anyway.
Yes, I agree with you.

Yes, I thank the minister. I want to say that under item 198, unemployment relief, we have for 1933-34 $2,600,000, and for last year we had $2,225,000. That is an increase of $375,000 this year. The families for whom I am speaking are families of returned men who cannot get one dollar of relief. I have had one particular letter from my own riding from a man with a family of eight who has had to haul cordwood into North Battleford, forty miles, in order to get enough for his family to live on, and the members of this family-as are many others- are not living as they should; they are simply on the verge of starvation. In this letter to me this man says that it is impossible to get any relief, and they have been practically starving all winter. Because this man has not got his pension established he cannot get a dollar to keep his family from starvation's door. Is there not something that the minister and his department can do in such a case? I think a case such as I have cited is a disgrace to Canada.
It is a disgrace to the government. It is not Canada that is responsible; it would do more.

Last fall when the house was in session the minister brought in a bill to amend the Canada Grain Act, to permit the 'Board of Grain Commissioners to make a change in the rates. Under that legislation I 'understand that the hoard changed the rate for storage from one-thirtieth to one forty-fifth of a cent per bushel. I have received communications asking whether it is possible for the board to reduce the spread between the Winnipeg price and the price paid the producer. Generally speaking, the freight rate in the west from many points in Manitoba and in eastern Saskatchewan is something like fifteen cents per bushel. The elevator com-
panies make a reduction from the Winnipeg price of twenty, twenty-one or twenty-two cents per bushel, giving the difference between the fifteen cenits and that twenty, twenty-one or twenty-two cents. May I ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce whether in his judgment the Board of Grain Commissioners under the present legislation have any means of dosing up that spread to some extent? There is a complaint in the west at the present time in that regard in view oif the low price of grain.

The answer to the first part of the question is that the Board of Grain Commissioners, under their powers extended by the grain act, and as is their duty, from year to year fix storage elevator rates. Last year they fixed one forty-fifth of a cent instead of one-thirtieth as a fair rate, but organizations, both cooperative and private, have represented that that reduction was not warranted and is improvident. The whole question will be considered by the board in July before the rate is fixed for next year, and a full hearing will be given. As regards the other part of the question, including the question of freight rates, all I can say is that the board has jurisdiction only in so far as eievator handling charges are concerned, and to the extent that they have jurisdiction they intend, as I learned talking to the chairman a few days ago, to give the whole matter careful consideration. All who desire to be heard will be heard before the rates for the next crop year are fixed.

The matter
which I am going to bring up now has been discussed in previous sessions, namely, the situation with respect to growers of durum wheat who delivered wheat to the Manitoba pool during the crop year 1930-31. I do not

Supply-Trade-Archives
wish to delay the 'house to-night, although it is causing considerable concern in a certain section of Manitoba; and I would not have brought it up had it not been that there was forwarded to me a letter in which the delegation representing the durum wheat growers of Manitoba apparently waited on the Minister of Trade and Commerce last fall. I presume he fully understands the situation. In the closing words of this communication they say:
Mr. Stevens was very interested in knowing what Mr. Bennett had said to us in the two interviews we had with him. We explained that he had asked us to wait for a while and give them time to sell all the balance of the wheat they were holding. Mr. Stevens told us that he sympathized with us very much but that he was in no position at present to make any promises. He promised that he would read our original letter to Mr. Bennett and also your resolution and that he would go into the matter as fully as he could with Mr. Bennett.
I want to ask the minister what answer he gave this committee when the occasion arose, and if he has not yet given an answer, what answer he is in a position to give.

The answer must be that which has already been given. What I said to them, and what I think all who have given consideration to the matter have also said, is that one sympathizes very much with the view taken by these producers of durum wheat. But their claim is against the pool in which they participated; there is no question about that. The Prime Minister is alleged to have said, as indicated by my hon. friend, that when the selling agency completed its sale of all holdings then possible, there would be some thing out of which the pool would be able to further compensate these growers, and that position still stands.

That is all very well, but I do not think it will satisfy these people, who in the first place contracted to deliver wheat to the Manitoba wheat pool, which was to turn it over to the central selling agency. Durum wheat at that time was selling slightly under common wheat, and the initial payment established for durum wheat was considerably below common wheat. Durum wheat that year, however, was all sold at a price considerably above common wheat-
That is quite right.

-and from a rought estimate I gather 'that it brought in about $500,000 more than was actually paid over to the grower. If it was dealt with on the same basis there would be roughly about 53719-319^
$200,000 coming to these people. I think the growers have a good claim to an adjustment, particularly with respect to the difference in the initial payments when the wheat was originally taken in. It is true that these farmers were contracted to deliver their wheat to the Manitoba pool, but a general change was made and Mr. McFarland was put in charge and the responsibility is now on the Dominion government. No accounting has been made of how this business has been handled and these people do not know exactly what is coming to them. Any figures presented are merely estimates and Mr. McFarland has given no real accounting. During the past two years I have taken up this matter on different occasions. I do not want to delay the proceedings at this late stage but I think this is of sufficient importance to be looked into and some action taken. This particular area in Manitoba where durum wheat is grown has been particularly hard hit during the past two years. The growers have suffered from causes other than not getting the full amount for their wheat, and I ask the minister to adjust this discrimination at the first opportunity.

best way to have it remedied is to disclose it. Until public opinion is created governments of all stripes are reluctant to act; they prefer to take the quiet attitude of hush, hush. They have done that continually in the past. When the great scandals in connection with brokerage firms of eastern Canada became known, you could not get the attorney general of Ontario to act, you could not get the attorney general of the province of Quebec to act. It was not until the province of Alberta took the bit in its teeth and ran away with the whole business of prosecuting Solloway and Mills, thereby showing the public the scandalous condition of *affairs, that the other provinces were compelled to act by virtue of the development of public opinion. speechtext: Yes.
We had better let this item stand until we have further information. This is too serious.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: Yes, but that is how the matter stood when we came into power; that is the situation.

The minister should
give the information to the committee. That is scandalous.

I would advise the
minister to bring his documents with him.
Documents of a verbal contract?

Mr. Chairman, you
will understand that we wish item 332 to stand.
Item stands.
Further amount to complete balance of payment for restoration of Saint John harbour, after the fire of 1931, including engineering and other services, not exceeding $50,000.
Let us have an explanation of this item. This is another fairly substantial sum; what is it for?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
I think the item is
well detailed in the estimate.
Is this the one for the harbour commission?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: Yes. As a matter of fact the work of reconstruction was done at very low cost, and this is the amount required for completion.
Is this a loan to the harbour commission, and will interest be charged on it the same as on other loans to harbour commissions?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: No, this will not be h loan to the commission.
Under whose jurisdiction was this money spent?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: This amount was spent under our own jurisdiction.
Any particular reason for that?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
Yes, we had some of our own employees supervise the work and

we had the engineering under our control. I can say to this committee that we have saved a large amount of money on that construction.
How much?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: Many thousands of dollars.
Was that under contract?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: It was cost plus four per cent, and the purpose was to control the whole thing, the engineering and the finances.
Who had the contract?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: Two firms had the contract, the Northern Construction company for a certain part of the works, and the Foundation Company, Limited, for the other part, at cost plus four per cent.

Mr. Chairman, I do not quite understand the situation that has developed at Saint John, in view of the fact that they have a harbour commission there to look after all the harbour work. The explanation that the minister has given is not clear to me as to the reason why the department went over the head of the harbour commission to construct certain works, or to even to supervise works being constructed. Is it usual for the department to do that where you have a harbour commission looking after the harbour works?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: It was unusual; it was due to the fact that as the committee knows a large fire had taken place there and we had to rebuild the whole thing within, I think, four months. As a matter of fact the whole construction was practically completed by the first of December, when the season of navigation opened. That is the reason the department came to the rescue of the harbour com-fnission. I think anyone who would go there and see the work that has been done for the *money expended will say that the job was done very cheaply.

Item 332, which the minister allowed to stand, was, he said, an inheritance from the previous government. I want to point out that the loan to the Chicoutimi 'harbour commission, described in this item, was authorized by the Chicoutimi Harbour Loan Act of 1931.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We are coming back to that item.

When the Minister of Marine brings down his papers to-morrow I would like him to note that the very money

Privilege-Mr. Gobeil
he is asking for is under the Chicoutimi Harbour Loan Act which did not come into force until 1931.
That item stands.
Mr. Chairman, I draw your attention to the fact that it is after eleven o'clock.
Let us go on by unanimous consent.

As the hon. gentleman has called attention to the time, I move that the committee rise and report progress.
Progress reported.
